source.title: Don't Cut Corners: Exact Conditions for Modularity in Biologically Inspired Representations
source.authors: Will Dorrell; Kyle Hsu; Luke Hollingsworth; Jin Hwa Lee; Jia-Jun Wu; Chelsea Finn; Peter E. Latham; T. Behrens; James C. R. Whittington

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures whether neurons in biologically constrained networks encode individual sources or mix them. This is a conceptual test of modularity, but it does not test the language-model neuron audits or explanation-prediction procedures in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper does not report an audit of neuron poles, named neuron explanations, held-out activation prediction, automated explanation scores, attribution graphs, or InceptionV1 cat-and-car. It reports its own modularity results for biologically constrained networks; results from cited studies are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study derives and tests when small, biologically constrained networks (nonnegative, energy-regularised) modularise or mix their encoding of known source variables. Its networks are toy autoencoders, a 25-unit feedforward net, a QLAE on Isaac3D, and small RNNs. It reports no neuron-pole audit, no language models, no InceptionV1 neurons, no attribution graphs and no explanation-prediction scoring. It frames itself within the modules-versus-mixtures debate in interpretability but never tests or uses the essay's claim. The record's 'tests/T2' should therefore be 'discusses/T6'.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. More precisely, the authors conclude that in biologically inspired (nonnegative, energy-efficient) networks, modularity is governed by range or support independence of the sources, not statistical independence. They give necessary and sufficient conditions for linear autoencoders and report that these predictions extend empirically to nonlinear feedforward networks and RNNs. They apply this to explain conflicting entorhinal grid-cell reward findings and to suggest non-classification origins of mixed selectivity.
record.recipe_differences: The study derives and evaluates modularity conditions for biologically constrained linear autoencoders and task-trained feedforward and recurrent networks; it does not use neuron explanation audits or held-out activation-prediction scoring.
record.method_sensitivity: Modularity changes with source-support conditions, particularly corner removal versus changes that preserve range independence; recurrent results also vary with frequency relationships and reward-position distributions.

fits_no_version.finding: In small task-trained networks, modular versus mixed neurons depend on the range or support of the source variables (corner cutting), much more than on statistical dependence. Optimal modularity is governed by a convex-hull/ellipse condition.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under nonnegativity and energy constraints, neurons modularise iff source support is sufficiently spread (range independence), not iff sources are statistically independent.

fits_no_version.finding: Without the biological constraints (ReLU positivity plus L2 activity and weight energy), the what-where network's neurons are mixed selective; with them, what and where separate (Appendix F.2, Figs 10–11). This is not recorded as a row.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activity and weight regularisation with nonnegativity is necessary for single-variable neurons in small feedforward networks. This is loosely analogous to V4's regularisation argument, but in a toy setting with no interpretable-share measure.

fits_no_version.finding: In a linear RNN tracking three correlated but range-independent objects, neurons are modular, yet appear mixed selective if one object is left out of the analysis (Fig 5, Appendix H.3). This is not recorded as a row.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Apparent mixed selectivity can be an artifact of unanalysed correlated variables. This is loosely analogous to V3's 'misread polysemanticity', but in a toy RNN rather than real models.

record.problems: The empirical results relevant to modularity are often described qualitatively in the text, without numerical values for the modularity scores. The experiments use task-trained, biologically constrained networks rather than pretrained language models or neuron-explanation audits.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results on modularity in the main text were omitted. Cited results from other studies were not recorded as rows.

untested.parts: Shares across other language models, dense and MoE, and scale.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose, recursive generalization versus superposition.
Interpretable-neuron share versus architecture, regularization and tools in real vision or language models. The paper's toy regularisation results are not this measure.
Neuron-based attribution graphs and reconstruction error.
Whether explanations from activating examples predict held-out activations.

record.verdict_notes: Off-topic for this phenomenon: no language or vision model neuron audits. The Appendix F.2 constraint-ablation and Fig 5 missed-variable results are noted under fits_no_version rather than missing, since they bear on no version directly.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B audit and its reported shares of one-job, two-job, and not-yet-understood neuron poles.
Shares across language models, dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, and model scale.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car and recursive generalization versus superposition.
Interpretability shares as a function of architecture, regularization, explanation tools, or vision-model size.
Attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons and their reconstruction error.
Whether explanations fitted to activating examples predict activations on new examples.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text.

rows.subject: optimal biologically inspired linear autoencoder
rows.operation_detail: Derives necessary and sufficient conditions for an optimal representation to modularise.

conditions.value: finite source samples; nonnegative activities; perfect linear reconstruction; L2 activity and weight costs

rows.measure: Whether each row of the input-weight matrix has at most one nonzero entry
rows.value: The optimal representation modularises if and only if the stated inequalities hold for all source-weight vectors; otherwise it is mixed.
rows.note: The result is conditional on the source sample and the stated linear-autoencoder assumptions; it gives no proportion of interpretable neurons.
rows.check: This is a theorem (necessary and sufficient conditions), not an empirical measurement. 'Observed' is not meaningful against any claim version.

rows.subject: What-Where Regression nonlinear feedforward network
rows.operation_detail: Trains with biologically inspired positivity and energy regularisation on source distributions with corner cutting.

conditions.value: independent what and where sources, then progressively cut corners

rows.baseline: The paper says the network begins modular when the sources are independent.
rows.value: Corner cutting increasingly degrades modularity; removing more than one corner data point causes mixed-selective neurons to appear.
rows.uncertainty: Standard error of the mean is shown in Figure 2; numerical values not stated.
rows.note: The text gives qualitative trends, not numerical CInfoM scores.
rows.check: The state 'partial' was assigned against no version. The row records corner cutting inducing mixing, a within-study comparison unrelated to any version's effect.

rows.subject: What-Where Regression nonlinear feedforward network
rows.operation_detail: Trains on diagonal-dropout source distributions while retaining range independence.

conditions.value: diagonal dropout; range boundary preserved

rows.value: Changing the distribution by removing diagonal examples affects modularity less than cutting corners; in the most extreme case, removing one data point from each corner is not sufficient to force mixed selectivity.
rows.uncertainty: Standard error of the mean is shown in Figure 2; numerical values not stated.
rows.note: The paper uses this condition as a comparison that changes statistical dependence without substantially changing range dependence.

rows.subject: What-Where Regression nonlinear feedforward network
rows.operation_detail: Trains on distributions with duplicated diagonal examples to correlate sources.

conditions.value: diagonal examples duplicated; range independence preserved

rows.value: Introducing correlations while preserving rectangular support causes less mixing than corner cutting with the same amount of mutual information.
rows.uncertainty: Standard error of the mean is shown in Figure 2; numerical values not stated.
rows.note: The comparison is described qualitatively; no numerical CInfoM values are stated in the text.

rows.subject: nonlinear autoencoder of source variables
rows.size_stated: six-dimensional latent bottleneck; three source dimensions
rows.operation_detail: Trains an autoencoder on source distributions with different support and correlation properties.

conditions.value: corner cutting

rows.value: Corner cutting induces substantially more latent mixing than introducing correlations while preserving rectangular support or removing central data.
rows.uncertainty: Standard error of the mean is shown in Figure 2; numerical values not stated.
rows.note: The text reports qualitative comparisons rather than numerical scores.

rows.subject: nonlinear autoencoder of source variables
rows.size_stated: six-dimensional latent bottleneck; three source dimensions
rows.operation_detail: Trains an autoencoder with source correlations while preserving rectangular support.

conditions.value: range-independent correlations

rows.value: This condition induces less latent mixing than corner cutting.
rows.uncertainty: Standard error of the mean is shown in Figure 2; numerical values not stated.
rows.note: The result is reported as a comparison with corner cutting.

rows.subject: nonlinear autoencoder of source variables
rows.size_stated: six-dimensional latent bottleneck; three source dimensions
rows.operation_detail: Trains an autoencoder after removing central data while preserving the support corners.

conditions.value: central data removed

rows.value: Removing central data induces less latent mixing than corner cutting.
rows.uncertainty: Standard error of the mean is shown in Figure 2; numerical values not stated.
rows.note: The result is reported as a qualitative comparison.

rows.subject: quantised latent autoencoder (QLAE) on Isaac3D
rows.operation_detail: Trains an image autoencoder on source distributions with corner cutting, range-independent correlations, or central-data removal.

conditions.value: subset of Isaac3D
corner cutting compared with range-independent correlations and central-data removal

rows.value: Corner cutting is a more important determinant of mixing than range-independent correlations or removal of centrally located data.
rows.uncertainty: Standard error of the mean is shown in Figure 2; numerical values not stated.
rows.note: The text reports the qualitative ordering, not numerical CInfoM values.

rows.note: The authors state that this result is empirically shown and proven in limited settings.

rows.subject: student ReLU RNN distilled from teacher RNN trajectories
rows.operation_detail: Trains students on teacher trajectories with controlled hidden-state source distributions.

conditions.value: statistical independence and range independence progressively broken

rows.note: The result is reported as qualitatively consistent with the theory.

rows.subject: student ReLU RNN distilled from teacher RNN trajectories
rows.operation_detail: Trains students on teacher trajectories with controlled hidden-state source distributions.

conditions.value: statistical independence, and to a lesser extent range independence, progressively broken

rows.value: Making corners sparse breaks modularity more slowly than removing corners.
rows.note: The paper reports a slower decline than in the corner-removal condition.

rows.subject: student ReLU RNN distilled from teacher RNN trajectories
rows.operation_detail: Trains students on teacher trajectories with controlled hidden-state source distributions.

conditions.value: only statistical independence progressively broken

rows.note: The paper reports the qualitative trend.

rows.subject: linear RNN for entorhinal spatial and reward-vector task
rows.operation_detail: Trains RNNs to report position and displacement from a reward across rooms with varying reward-position distributions.

conditions.value: some rooms have randomly placed rewards; fixed-reward rooms are also present

rows.measure: Whether neurons encode spatial and reward variables separately or mix them
rows.value: The representation remains modular until all sampled rooms have fixed reward positions.
rows.note: The paper states that the modular representation contains separate spatial and reward-vector cells.

rows.subject: linear RNN for entorhinal spatial and reward-vector task
rows.operation_detail: Trains an RNN to report position and displacement from a reward.

conditions.value: all sampled rooms have fixed reward positions

rows.measure: Whether neurons encode spatial and reward variables separately or mix them
rows.value: Neurons become mixed selective to reward and self-position.
rows.note: The paper reports mixing at this distributional extreme.
rows.check: 'Partial' does not apply: the paper reports full mixing when all rooms are fixed, and this bears on no version.
